title: Banking: central banks and commercial banks

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define commercial banks and the central bank, and explain their role and importance for government, producers and consumers.

blocks.heading: Commercial banks
blocks.text: A commercial bank is a financial institution that accepts deposits from households and firms, lends the pooled funds to borrowers, and moves payments between accounts. Namib Signs of Walvis Bay keeps its takings in a current account, pays its three suppliers by transfer and borrows N$250 000 for a new printing machine; around the account stand the services a commercial bank provides - safekeeping for deposits, loans, and payments moved at a distance. A family firm in Rotterdam uses its bank in the same three ways, which shows the role travels beyond Namibia.

blocks.heading: The central bank
blocks.text: A central bank is the institution at the centre of a country's banking system; in Namibia that is the Bank of Namibia, and the euro area's equivalent sits in Frankfurt, Germany. A central bank issues the notes and coins, holds the government's account and settles its payments, keeps the deposits of the commercial banks, and stands behind them as lender of last resort when deposits are withdrawn in a rush.

blocks.heading: More jobs of the central bank
blocks.text: Beyond issuing notes, banking for the government and holding the commercial banks' deposits, a central bank does further jobs. It sets the interest rate at which it lends to commercial banks; in Namibia this is the Bank of Namibia's repo rate. When it raises that rate, commercial banks tend to raise the rates they charge on loans and pay on savings, and when it cuts the rate they tend to follow it down. It manages the country's reserves of foreign currency, and where the currency is fixed it uses them to hold the exchange rate: the Namibian dollar is held at one-for-one with the South African rand, so the Bank of Namibia tends to move its repo rate in step with South Africa's central bank and holds reserves to back the peg. And it supervises the commercial banks, setting rules on how much they must keep in reserve and checking how they lend, so that deposits stay safe. How interest rates are used to steer the whole economy is taught in topic 4.4.

blocks.heading: Two banks, two customers
blocks.text: The boundary between them is who they serve. A commercial bank serves households and firms: it takes their deposits and makes them loans. The central bank serves the government and the commercial banks themselves, and does not open accounts for private customers - a worker in Oshakati banks with a commercial bank, while the government banks with the Bank of Namibia.

blocks.heading: Why each matters, and to whom
blocks.text: For producers: banks pool many small deposits into larger loans, so Kaoko Juice of Oshakati can borrow N$400 000 for bottling equipment that no single saver could finance, and bridge the weeks between paying for fruit and receiving juice revenue. For consumers: deposits are safer than notes kept at home and payments travel to a school in Gobabis without cash moving. For government: taxes and civil-service salaries move through accounts at the central bank and the commercial banks, so collections and payments have a channel. For the economy: the payments linking buyers and sellers run on this system.

blocks.heading: Why the central bank matters to producers and consumers
blocks.text: The central bank seldom deals with producers and consumers directly, but its work reaches them in several ways. A currency people trust lets a shop in Rundu price its goods in Namibian dollars and lets a worker accept a wage paid in them. Its interest rate changes the cost of borrowing: if the repo rate rises by one percentage point, a firm with a N$500 000 loan whose rate follows it pays about N$5 000 more interest a year, households pay more on car and home loans, and savers earn more. Its supervision makes it less likely that a bank fails with customers' savings inside. And as lender of last resort it can lend to a bank facing a rush of withdrawals, so wages, supplier payments and card payments keep flowing instead of freezing. For the government the central bank is banker and note-issuer; for producers and consumers it is much of the reason money and banks can be trusted.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The government's budget in topic 4.3 is paid and collected through these accounts, and the role of the state that stands over them is examined in topic 4.1.
